source_text: As President Donald Trump’s approval rating plunges to a historic low of 36 percent, experts have an increasingly dismal assessment of his second administration. “This is what a crater looks like in politics,” said pollster and political analyst Cornell Belcher . “By every key objective measure this is clearly a failed presidency.” Trump’s approval rating was already low, but his latest drop is among the sharpest declines of either of his terms. It comes as he confronts a series of crises largely of his own making. The first is the economy. In 2024, voters overwhelmingly ranked the economy as their top concern — its strongest influence since the Great Recession of 2008. Cost of living skyrocketed in the wake of COVID-19, and while then-President Joe Biden’s administration reduced inflation and rebounded the economy faster than any other nation , a financially rattled electorate voted for Trump thinking his economic approach would outperform that of Kamala Harris, who was widely viewed as a continuation of Biden. But voter hopes haven’t panned out. Today, only 29 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s economic stewardship, while just 25 percent approve of his handling of the cost of living. “It’s important that people know that the president feels their pain and that help is on the way,” said Amanda Makki, a Republican political strategist and lawyer. Trump hasn’t exactly delivered on that, famously making obtuse statements like “maybe the children will have 2 dolls instead of 30 ” as the economy soured under the weight of his tariffs. What’s more, the fact that gas prices are approaching record highs not only says something about the Trump economy, but links to the second major reason Americans are displeased with the president: his war on Iran. Just 35 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s actions in Iran, down from 37 percent a week ago. Only 26 percent agree with Trump’s assertion that the war will make the U.S. safer, and a mere 7 percent support his suggestion of putting boots on the ground. And with gas prices spiking up to a national average just shy of $4 and no clear end in sight to the war, Americans are not happy with how Trump’s military “excursion” is hurting them at the pump. Trump may dismiss concerns over affordability as a “Democratic hoax,” but voters aren’t buying it.

Trump’s approval rating was already weak, but the latest decline ranks among the sharpest drops of either of his terms. The collapse comes as he faces a series of crises that critics say his own decisions helped create.

The economy is the first and most immediate problem. In 2024, voters overwhelmingly identified the economy as their top concern, making it the strongest electoral influence since the Great Recession of 2008. After COVID-19 sent the cost of living soaring, the Biden administration reduced inflation and saw the economy rebound faster than any other nation. Still, a financially battered electorate turned to Trump, believing his economic approach would outperform that of Kamala Harris, who was widely viewed as a continuation of Biden.

Those expectations have not been met. Trump has not delivered that reassurance. Instead, as tariffs have weighed on the economy, he has made dismissive and tone-deaf comments such as, “maybe the children will have 2 dolls instead of 30.”

Rising gas prices have further exposed the consequences of the administration’s policies. Prices are approaching record highs, adding to the second major source of public anger: Trump’s war on Iran. Just 35 percent of Americans approve of his actions in Iran, down from 37 percent a week earlier. Only 26 percent agree with Trump’s claim that the war will make the United States safer, and just 7 percent support his suggestion of putting boots on the ground.

With gas prices surging to a national average just shy of $4 and no clear end to the war, Americans are increasingly frustrated that Trump’s military “excursion” is imposing additional costs on families at the pump. Still, new operators like Filmhouse taking over The Projector and the presence of around 30 cinema locations islandwide show that the big screen experience isn’t gone yet, even if it doesn’t look the same as before. #8dayssg #8dayssgtrending #singapore #sgnews #cinema

source_text:
Golden Village has announced that its Tiong Bahru Plaza outlet will close at the end of March 2026, after more than 30 years of serving Singapore moviegoers. Its closure makes it one of the country’s oldest cinemas to shut in recent years, marking another loss for a longstanding communal and family space—one that gave people a shared cultural experience beyond the isolation of home entertainment.

The decision adds to a growing list of theatres that have disappeared, including Shaw Seletar, Cathay Cineplexes locations, and The Projector’s former Golden Mile venue. Streaming platforms and changing audience habits continue to reshape how people spend their leisure time, placing traditional cinemas under pressure and weakening the shared public experiences that once brought communities together. Convenience may be winning, but it comes at the cost of traditions and places that encouraged people to gather together.

Still, the big screen has not vanished. New operators such as Filmhouse, which took over The Projector, and around 30 cinema locations islandwide show that Singapore’s cinema tradition remains. It may look different from the past, but the enduring appeal of gathering in a theatre to watch a film together is not gone yet.

Many of the new believers in Softcare Ltd. (2698.HK) cheered the release of the company's inaugural annual results late last week by bidding up its shares nearly 15% in the two trading days after the announcement. The company's revenue rose by 24.9% year-over-year to $567 million last year, while its net profit was up 27.4% to $121 million. Its gross profit margin also rose from 35.2% in 2024 to 35.9% in 2025, another positive indicator. Sales to its core markets in Africa rose by a healthy 22.5% to $545 million. The company is also moving out of Africa to find success in other emerging markets. The best example is Latin America, whose sales more than doubled to $22 million, just five years after it entered Peru in 2020, and added El Salvador in 2024. The company is also building a presence in Central Asia, where its sales, though quite small, more than doubled last year to $272,000. After several years of declines, average selling prices (ASP) for Softcare's two largest product lines rose between 4% and 7% last year, according to the results announcement. Baby diaper ASPs increased by 4.4% year-over-year, as that segment accounted for 78.6% of total revenue. Feminine hygiene product ASPs grew by 7% and made up 17.5% of revenue. rewritten_text:
Softcare delivered a strong first full-year performance as a publicly listed company, demonstrating that disciplined attention to core markets and practical consumer needs can outperform skeptics. Revenue rose 24.9% year over year to $567 million last year, while net profit increased 27.4% to $121 million. Gross profit margin also improved, rising from 35.2% in 2024 to 35.9% in 2025.

The company, widely known as the “African diaper king,” reported 25% revenue growth, led by a 134% increase in Latin America and double-digit growth across its established African markets. The results place the diaper maker at the forefront of a new wave of Chinese companies seeking to serve consumers in Africa and other emerging markets.

Softcare Ltd. (2698.HK) has defied skeptics who questioned whether it could maintain its dominant position in Africa and build a durable business in newer markets. Investors responded favorably to the release of the company’s inaugural annual results late last week, bidding its shares up nearly 15% over the following two trading days.

Sales in Softcare’s core African markets rose a healthy 22.5% to $545 million. The company is also expanding beyond Africa, with Latin America providing the clearest example of its progress. Sales there more than doubled to $22 million, only five years after the company entered Peru in 2020 and later added El Salvador in 2024.

Softcare is also establishing a presence in Central Asia. Although sales there remain small, they more than doubled last year to $272,000.

After several years of declines, average selling prices for Softcare’s two largest product lines increased between 4% and 7% last year, according to the results announcement. Baby diaper prices rose 4.4% year over year, with that segment accounting for 78.6% of total revenue. Feminine hygiene product prices increased 7% and represented 17.5% of revenue.

These price increases are significant because they indicate that Softcare is persuading consumers to pay more for its products in highly price-sensitive markets. That ability is helping the company preserve and even strengthen its margins through sound commercial discipline rather than relying solely on volume growth.

In a previous prospectus issued before its November IPO last year, Softcare reported that profit growth had slowed to 54.1% in the first three quarters of 2024, down from explosive growth of 252% in 2023. A later filing showed that profit growth slowed further, to just 12% in the first four months ... Full story available on Benzinga.com

source_text:
Softcare delivered a strong first full-year performance as a publicly listed company, demonstrating that disciplined attention to core markets and practical consumer needs can outperform skeptics. Revenue rose 24.9% year over year to $567 million last year, while net profit increased 27.4% to $121 million. Gross profit margin also improved, rising from 35.2% in 2024 to 35.9% in 2025.

The company, widely known as the “African diaper king,” reported 25% revenue growth, led by a 134% increase in Latin America and double-digit growth across its established African markets. The results place the diaper maker at the forefront of a new wave of Chinese companies seeking to serve consumers in Africa and other emerging markets.

Softcare Ltd. (2698.HK) has defied skeptics who questioned whether it could maintain its dominant position in Africa and build a durable business in newer markets. Investors responded favorably to the release of the company’s inaugural annual results late last week, bidding its shares up nearly 15% over the following two trading days.

Sales in Softcare’s core African markets rose a healthy 22.5% to $545 million. The company is also expanding beyond Africa, with Latin America providing the clearest example of its progress. Sales there more than doubled to $22 million, only five years after the company entered Peru in 2020 and later added El Salvador in 2024.

Softcare is also establishing a presence in Central Asia. Although sales there remain small, they more than doubled last year to $272,000.

After several years of declines, average selling prices for Softcare’s two largest product lines increased between 4% and 7% last year, according to the results announcement. Baby diaper prices rose 4.4% year over year, with that segment accounting for 78.6% of total revenue. Feminine hygiene product prices increased 7% and represented 17.5% of revenue.

These price increases are significant because they indicate that Softcare is persuading consumers to pay more for its products in highly price-sensitive markets. That ability is helping the company preserve and even strengthen its margins through sound commercial discipline rather than relying solely on volume growth.

In a previous prospectus issued before its November IPO last year, Softcare reported that profit growth had slowed to 54.1% in the first three quarters of 2024, down from explosive growth of 252% in 2023. source_text: Delhi PWD Accelerates PNG Pipeline Laying with 24-Hour Approvals In a bid to expedite infrastructure development for cleaner fuel access, the Delhi Public Works Department (PWD) has announced a significant policy shift. Effective immediately, road-cutting permissions for laying PNG pipelines by Indraprastha Gas Limited (IGL) will be approved within 24 hours of receiving a complete request. The department, responsible for overseeing the capital's road infrastructure, has also waived road restoration charges for the next three months until June 30, 2026. This move aims to accelerate the installation of PNG connections by removing financial and bureaucratic hurdles. Officials emphasized that IGL is expected to prioritize this task, ensuring swift work completion supported by adequate manpower. Additionally, the areas excavated during pipeline installation must be backfilled securely to avoid public hazards. This initiative highlights the government's commitment to improving public access to cleaner energy in Delhi.

Officials stressed that IGL must treat the work as a priority, deploy sufficient manpower, and complete projects without unnecessary delay. Excavated areas must be securely backfilled to protect the public, particularly those who rely on safe and accessible roads, and to preserve orderly public infrastructure. The initiative reflects an effort to make essential services more responsive, reduce administrative obstacles, and extend cleaner energy through stronger public infrastructure.
